questions.stem:
A 29-year-old man who grew up on a pig farm in rural Mexico and moved to New Jersey 4 years ago is brought to the emergency department after a seizure. He has had intermittent headaches for months. MRI of the brain shows several small viable cysts in the brain parenchyma with mild surrounding edema. Serology for the suspected tapeworm is positive. He is started on an antiseizure medication.

Which additional regimen is most appropriate?
choices: Praziquantel alone as a single dose
Ivermectin with doxycycline
Corticosteroids and albendazole
Triclabendazole alone
Metronidazole with paromomycin

explain.html:
Neurocysticercosis (NCC) is infection of the central nervous system after ingestion of Taenia solium eggs, and its picture depends on cyst size, stage, location, viability and the host response. The two most common presentations are seizures and raised intracranial pressure. Intraparenchymal disease (over 60% of cases) causes seizures and headache, while ventricular or subarachnoid cysts cause hydrocephalus and carry higher mortality. Diagnosis rests on imaging and serology, sometimes biopsy.

This man grew up on a pig farm in an endemic area and now has seizures, headaches, several viable parenchymal cysts with edema and positive serology. Treatment is complicated, but the regimen is corticosteroids plus albendazole: killing viable cysts provokes inflammation around them, which the steroids blunt. Single-dose praziquantel is the treatment for the intestinal adult (taeniasis), not for cysts in the brain.
why: Single-dose praziquantel treats the adult tapeworm in the intestine, not cysticerci in the brain.
Ivermectin with doxycycline is the regimen for onchocerciasis.
Triclabendazole is a fluke drug and is not part of the cestode regimens taught for NCC.
Metronidazole with paromomycin treats amebiasis.
explain.takeaway: Neurocysticercosis presents with seizures or raised intracranial pressure, is diagnosed by imaging and serology, and is treated with corticosteroids plus albendazole; praziquantel is for intestinal taeniasis.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Describe the presentation, diagnosis and treatment of neurocysticercosis.

rows.why: Single-dose praziquantel treats the adult tapeworm in the intestine, not cysticerci in the brain.
rows.if_right: proglottids in the stool with only mild GI symptoms (intestinal taeniasis)

rows.why: Ivermectin with doxycycline is the regimen for onchocerciasis.
rows.if_right: skin nodules, severe itching and eye scarring in a West African farmer (river blindness)

rows.why: Triclabendazole is a fluke drug and is not part of the cestode regimens taught for NCC.
rows.if_right: a liver fluke infection acquired from raw watercress

rows.why: Metronidazole with paromomycin treats amebiasis.
rows.if_right: bloody diarrhea with a liver abscess and flask-shaped colonic ulcers

questions.stem:
A 48-year-old man who grew up herding sheep in the Middle East with the help of several dogs is brought to the emergency department after a motorcycle crash with blunt trauma to the right upper abdomen. Within minutes he develops diffuse hives, lip swelling, wheezing, and hypotension. He has received no medications or contrast. CT of the abdomen shows a large cyst in the right lobe of the liver with smaller daughter cysts along its inner wall and fluid around the liver.

Which of the following best explains his acute deterioration?
choices: Release of cyst fluid causing a systemic allergic reaction
Bacterial superinfection of the cyst with septic shock
Rupture of an amebic liver abscess into the peritoneum
Hemorrhage into the peritoneum from a cholangiocarcinoma at the hilum
Disseminated larvae carrying enteric bacteria into blood

explain.html:
Echinococcus causes hydatid cyst disease. Dogs carry the adult tapeworm in the small intestine and pass eggs in feces; sheep (and goats, camels, cattle, swine) ingest the eggs, and humans are incidental hosts who do the same. The larvae migrate from the GI tract through the blood to the liver or lung, where they grow into a large cyst with daughter vesicles; most cysts are asymptomatic until about 10 cm.

The danger is rupture after trauma, which spills highly antigenic cyst fluid and causes an allergic reaction that can progress to anaphylaxis. This sheep herder who worked with dogs took a blow to the right upper abdomen, has a liver cyst with daughter cysts and free fluid, and develops hives, lip swelling, wheeze and hypotension within minutes without any drug or contrast. That timing and the allergic features point to cyst fluid, not infection or bleeding.
why: Septic shock develops over hours with fever and does not cause hives, lip swelling and wheeze within minutes.
An amebic abscess has no daughter cysts and its rupture causes peritonitis, not an allergic reaction.
A hilar cholangiocarcinoma does not explain daughter cysts, and hemorrhage causes pallor and shock without urticaria.
Larvae carrying enteric bacteria into the blood is disseminated Strongyloides, which follows immunosuppression, not trauma.
explain.takeaway: Traumatic rupture of an Echinococcus hydatid cyst releases antigenic fluid that can cause anaphylaxis, so cysts are not punctured or ruptured casually.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Describe the life cycle and complications of Echinococcus hydatid cyst disease, including anaphylaxis after cyst rupture.

rows.why: Septic shock develops over hours with fever and does not cause hives, lip swelling and wheeze within minutes.
rows.if_right: fever and rigors days after a cyst became secondarily infected

rows.why: An amebic abscess has no daughter cysts and its rupture causes peritonitis, not an allergic reaction.
rows.if_right: bloody diarrhea followed by a single liver abscess with anchovy paste contents

rows.why: A hilar cholangiocarcinoma does not explain daughter cysts, and hemorrhage causes pallor and shock without urticaria.
rows.if_right: painless jaundice with a hilar mass in a patient with long-standing liver fluke infection

rows.why: Larvae carrying enteric bacteria into the blood is disseminated Strongyloides, which follows immunosuppression, not trauma.
rows.if_right: gram-negative bacteremia after high-dose steroids in a patient with chronic larva currens

questions.stem:
A 6-year-old girl is brought to the clinic because she has been scratching her bottom at night and waking up crying for 2 weeks. Her younger brother has started doing the same. She attends a full-day kindergarten. Examination of the perianal skin shows excoriations. Stool ova and parasite examination sent by another clinic last week was negative.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?
choices: Repeat stool ova and parasite examination on three separate days
Serum antibody testing for the suspected nematode
Clear adhesive tape applied to the perianal skin on waking
Blood smear collected at midnight
Biopsy of the excoriated perianal skin

explain.html:
Pinworm (Enterobius vermicularis) is the most common helminth in the United States, affecting children, institutionalized adults and caretakers, and humans are its only host. Ingested eggs mature into adults in the cecum, and the females exit the anus at night to lay eggs on the perianal skin, which causes the intense nocturnal itching. Eggs then sit on hands, toys, bedding and toilets for 1 to 2 weeks, so the infection spreads through households and classrooms.

Because the eggs are on the skin and not in the stool, O&P is not helpful, which explains this girl's negative test. The diagnosis is the scotch tape test, which picks up transparent eggs flattened on one side, collected from the perianal skin on waking or 2 to 3 hours after sleep. Treatment is albendazole, repeated 2 weeks later, with hot-water laundering and drying.
why: Repeating stool exams does not help because pinworm eggs are laid on the perianal skin, not passed in feces.
Serology is not the test for pinworm, which is found by collecting eggs from the skin.
A midnight blood smear finds Wuchereria or Brugia microfilariae, not pinworm.
Biopsy is invasive and unnecessary because the eggs sit on the skin surface.
explain.takeaway: Pinworm causes nocturnal perianal itching; diagnose it with the scotch tape test (stool O&P is negative) and treat with albendazole repeated in 2 weeks.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Describe the transmission, diagnosis and treatment of Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm).

rows.why: Repeating stool exams does not help because pinworm eggs are laid on the perianal skin, not passed in feces.
rows.if_right: Strongyloides, where O&P has poor sensitivity and three samples are needed

rows.why: Serology is not the test for pinworm, which is found by collecting eggs from the skin.
rows.if_right: Toxocara or Strongyloides, which are diagnosed by antibody testing

rows.why: A midnight blood smear finds Wuchereria or Brugia microfilariae, not pinworm.
rows.if_right: progressive leg lymphedema after mosquito exposure in an endemic region

rows.why: Biopsy is invasive and unnecessary because the eggs sit on the skin surface.
rows.if_right: a skin nodule needing a skin snip, as in onchocerciasis

questions.stem:
A 5-year-old girl in a tropical village with poor sanitation is brought to a clinic with chronic diarrhea streaked with blood, abdominal pain, and weight loss. While straining she develops a protrusion of pink, worm-studded rectal mucosa through the anus. Stool microscopy shows barrel-shaped eggs with a plug at each end.

Where do the adult worms causing this condition live?
choices: Jejunum, attached by a scolex
Lymphatic vessels of the pelvis and legs
Bile ducts of the liver
Large intestine, cecum, and appendix
Pulmonary alveoli and bronchi

explain.html:
The whipworm, Trichuris trichiura, is acquired by ingesting food, water or soil contaminated with feces that contain eggs. The adults are 3 to 5 cm and live in the large intestine, cecum and appendix. Infection causes abdominal pain, bloody stool, diarrhea and weight loss, and heavy infection in children can lead to rectal prolapse.

This girl has bloody diarrhea, weight loss and a worm-studded rectal prolapse, and her stool shows barrel-shaped eggs with plugged ends, which identifies whipworm. Diagnosis is stool O&P, and treatment is albendazole together with avoiding contaminated food and water.
why: A scolex attaching to the small intestine is how tapeworms live; whipworm is a roundworm of the colon.
Lymphatic vessels house Wuchereria and Brugia, which cause lymphedema, not bloody diarrhea.
Bile ducts are not the home of whipworm and would cause biliary, not colonic, disease.
The alveoli hold migrating larvae of Ascaris, hookworm and Strongyloides, never adult whipworms.
explain.takeaway: Trichuris adults live in the large intestine, cecum and appendix, cause bloody diarrhea and rectal prolapse in children, and have eggs with plugged ends; treat with albendazole.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Describe Trichuris trichiura (whipworm): habitat, presentation, egg morphology and treatment.

rows.why: A scolex attaching to the small intestine is how tapeworms live; whipworm is a roundworm of the colon.
rows.if_right: flat proglottids in the stool after eating undercooked pork, beef or fish

rows.why: Lymphatic vessels house Wuchereria and Brugia, which cause lymphedema, not bloody diarrhea.
rows.if_right: progressive leg swelling with microfilariae in blood drawn at night

rows.why: Bile ducts are not the home of whipworm and would cause biliary, not colonic, disease.
rows.if_right: jaundice from a fluke living in the biliary tree

rows.why: The alveoli hold migrating larvae of Ascaris, hookworm and Strongyloides, never adult whipworms.
rows.if_right: wheeze with transient infiltrates and eosinophilia (Loeffler syndrome)

questions.stem:
A 33-year-old woman comes to the clinic 1 week after returning from a beach vacation in the Caribbean, where she walked barefoot on the sand every day. She has an intensely itchy, raised, red, serpiginous track on the sole of her right foot that she says has moved a few centimeters each day. She feels otherwise well and has no cough, diarrhea, or anemia.

Which of the following best describes this condition?
choices: Dog or cat hookworm larvae that cannot complete their cycle in humans
Human hookworm larvae that will mature into adults in the gut
Strongyloides larvae autoinfecting through the perianal skin
Filarial adult worms migrating through subcutaneous connective tissue
Schistosome cercariae causing a delayed egg granuloma

explain.html:
Hookworm larvae in soil or sand penetrate bare skin. The human hookworms (Necator, Ancylostoma duodenale) go on through the blood and lungs to the gut, but dog or cat hookworm larvae (usually Ancylostoma species) cannot complete their cycle in people. They wander in the skin, producing cutaneous larva migrans: an itchy, raised, erythematous serpiginous track that moves.

The track appears 1 to 5 days (up to a month) after penetration, the larva dies within 5 to 6 weeks, and there are no long-term effects. This woman walked barefoot on a Caribbean beach and has a moving foot track with no cough, diarrhea or anemia, which fits an animal hookworm stuck in the skin rather than a human hookworm reaching the gut.
why: Human hookworms travel to the lungs and gut and cause anemia, which she does not have.
Strongyloides autoinfection causes larva currens, recurrent fast streaks on the trunk or buttocks in chronic infection.
Filarial adults migrating in subcutaneous tissue (Loa loa) cause painless Calabar swellings, not a thin track on the sole.
Schistosome cercariae are a freshwater, not beach sand, exposure, and their disease comes from eggs in viscera.
explain.takeaway: Cutaneous larva migrans is a self-limited, migrating, itchy skin track from dog or cat hookworm larvae that cannot mature in humans and die in 5 to 6 weeks.
explain.topic: Cutaneous larva migrans: humans as dead-end hosts
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Describe cutaneous larva migrans caused by dog or cat hookworm larvae.

rows.why: Human hookworms travel to the lungs and gut and cause anemia, which she does not have.
rows.if_right: months later, iron deficiency anemia and eggs in the stool after the skin rash

rows.why: Strongyloides autoinfection causes larva currens, recurrent fast streaks on the trunk or buttocks in chronic infection.
rows.if_right: years of recurrent linear streaks on the buttocks with epigastric pain after living in Appalachia

rows.why: Filarial adults migrating in subcutaneous tissue (Loa loa) cause painless Calabar swellings, not a thin track on the sole.
rows.if_right: migrating painless swellings and a worm crossing the eye in a Central African resident

rows.why: Schistosome cercariae are a freshwater, not beach sand, exposure, and their disease comes from eggs in viscera.
rows.if_right: hematuria months after swimming in Lake Victoria

questions.stem:
A 52-year-old woman who emigrated from a tropical country 20 years ago is being evaluated before starting a biologic agent for rheumatoid arthritis. She reports occasional epigastric discomfort and recurring, rapidly moving, itchy linear streaks across her lower trunk. Her peripheral eosinophil count is mildly elevated. A single stool ova and parasite examination is negative. She is also found to be positive for human T-lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1).

Which of the following is the most appropriate approach?
choices: No action is needed, because the stool examination was negative
Praziquantel, with a stool recheck in 6 weeks
Albendazole single dose, repeated after 2 weeks
Serology, and treatment with ivermectin before the biologic
Diethylcarbamazine after a daytime blood smear

explain.html:
Chronic Strongyloides infection can last for decades through autoinfection and is often mild: epigastric pain, intermittent diarrhea or constipation, about 75% with mild eosinophilia, and recurrent larva currens. The danger appears when immunosuppression begins, because HTLV-1, high-dose corticosteroids, biologics, chemotherapy, malignancy and HIV are risk factors for dissemination, which is fatal in 50 to 90%.

The diagnostic trap is that stool O&P has poor sensitivity (three are needed), so one negative exam excludes nothing. Serology is the better test, and treatment is ivermectin. This woman from the tropics has larva currens, eosinophilia, HTLV-1 and a planned biologic, so she needs testing and treatment first, because prevention is the whole point.
explain.table:
OrganismWhy stool O&P failsTest to use
EchinococcusHumans carry only the larval cystImaging (US, CT) and serology
EnterobiusEggs laid on perianal skinScotch tape test
ToxocaraLarvae never mature in the human gutSerology (ELISA)
StrongyloidesPoor sensitivity, needs 3 samplesSerology
TrichinellaLarvae encyst in muscleSerum antibody, muscle biopsy
why: One negative stool exam is insensitive for Strongyloides, and starting a biologic on an untreated infection risks fatal dissemination.
Praziquantel treats tapeworms and flukes, not Strongyloides.
Albendazole repeated after 2 weeks is the pinworm regimen.
Diethylcarbamazine after a daytime smear is the approach to Loa loa.
explain.takeaway: Chronic Strongyloides is best diagnosed by serology because stool O&P is insensitive, and it is treated with ivermectin before steroids or biologics, especially with HTLV-1.
explain.topic: Strongyloides: diagnosis and treatment of chronic infection
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Describe the diagnosis, treatment and prevention of Strongyloides infection before immunosuppression.

rows.why: One negative stool exam is insensitive for Strongyloides, and starting a biologic on an untreated infection risks fatal dissemination.
rows.if_right: no symptoms, no eosinophilia and no epidemiologic risk for Strongyloides

rows.why: Praziquantel treats tapeworms and flukes, not Strongyloides.
rows.if_right: proglottids in the stool from an intestinal tapeworm

rows.why: Albendazole repeated after 2 weeks is the pinworm regimen.
rows.if_right: a child with nocturnal perianal itching and a positive scotch tape test

rows.why: Diethylcarbamazine after a daytime smear is the approach to Loa loa.
rows.if_right: Calabar swellings and daytime microfilariae in a Central African resident

questions.stem:
A 26-year-old man living in Hawaii is brought to the emergency department with 2 days of severe headache, neck stiffness, fever, and burning paresthesias in his legs. Five days earlier he ate a salad made from lettuce from his backyard garden, where slugs and snails are common. Laboratory studies show:

[[labs 0]]

Which of the following is the most likely cause?
choices: Naegleria fowleri
Angiostrongylus cantonensis
Taenia solium
Toxocara canis
Trichinella spiralis

explain.html:
Eosinophilic meningitis is defined as more than 10 eosinophils/mm3 or more than 10% eosinophils in the CSF. Its main causes are Angiostrongylus and Baylisascaris, ahead of Toxocara. In each, humans are accidental hosts: ingested larvae travel to the CNS, get stuck, die and trigger eosinophilic inflammation, and all treatment is supportive.

The exposure picks the worm. Angiostrongylus cantonensis, the rat lungworm, comes from snails or slugs on produce, or infected crab or shrimp, in Southeast Asia, the Caribbean, Hawaii and the southern US, and most cases are self-limited. This man in Hawaii ate lettuce from a garden full of slugs and snails, and has headache, neck stiffness, paresthesias and 18% CSF eosinophils.
explain.table:
CauseExposureMain syndrome
Angiostrongylus cantonensis (rat lungworm)Snails, slugs, produce, crab, shrimp; SE Asia, Caribbean, Hawaii, southern USEosinophilic (aseptic) meningitis, usually self-limited
Baylisascaris procyonis (raccoon roundworm)Raccoon feces, sandboxes, garbage; northeast and Midwest US, CanadaEosinophilic meningitis; neural, ocular, visceral larva migrans
Toxocara (dog, cat roundworm)Soil, sand, puppies, picaVisceral, ocular, neural larva migrans; less often meningitis
why: Naegleria causes fulminant meningoencephalitis after freshwater swimming, without CSF eosinophilia.
Taenia solium causes neurocysticercosis with seizures and brain cysts, not eosinophilic meningitis after a salad.
Toxocara is a less common cause of eosinophilic meningitis and fits a young child with pica and puppies.
Trichinella causes myalgia, periorbital edema and eosinophilia after undercooked wild-game meat.
explain.takeaway: Eosinophilic meningitis after eating produce contaminated by snails or slugs in Hawaii, the Caribbean or the southern US is Angiostrongylus cantonensis, and treatment is supportive.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Identify the causes of eosinophilic meningitis and their exposures.

rows.if_right: rapid deterioration after lake swimming with amebae seen in the CSF

rows.why: Taenia solium causes neurocysticercosis with seizures and brain cysts, not eosinophilic meningitis after a salad.
rows.if_right: seizures with ring-enhancing parenchymal cysts in someone from a pig-raising area

rows.why: Toxocara is a less common cause of eosinophilic meningitis and fits a young child with pica and puppies.
rows.if_right: a toddler with pica, puppies, hepatomegaly and very high blood eosinophils

rows.why: Trichinella causes myalgia, periorbital edema and eosinophilia after undercooked wild-game meat.
rows.if_right: fever, severe myalgia and periorbital edema after eating rare bear meat

questions.stem:
A 7-year-old girl is brought to the ophthalmologist because her teacher noticed she could not see the board with her right eye. Her parents report no fever or other illness. She plays daily in a sandbox shared with neighborhood cats and dogs. Examination shows decreased vision in the right eye only, with a whitish mass on the retina and surrounding chorioretinitis. The left eye is normal. The peripheral eosinophil count is normal. A pediatric oncologist is consulted because of concern for a retinal tumor.

Which of the following is the most likely cause?
choices: Larvae of a dog or cat roundworm lodged in the eye
Microfilariae of a black fly-borne worm in the eye
An adult worm migrating beneath the conjunctiva
Free-living amebae infecting the cornea
Tapeworm cysts lodged in the vitreous after eating pork

explain.html:
Toxocara larvae from dog or cat feces in soil and sand cause three forms of disease. Ocular toxocariasis (ocular larva migrans) mostly affects children 5 to 10 years old and is usually unilateral: a single larva penetrates one eye and causes decreased vision, uveitis and chorioretinitis.

Two features make it a trap. It can be misdiagnosed as retinoblastoma, and there is often no systemic involvement, so a normal eosinophil count does not exclude it. This 7-year-old who plays in a sandbox shared with cats and dogs has vision loss in one eye with a whitish retinal mass and chorioretinitis, and the oncology consult reflects exactly that mimicry. Treatment aims to minimize damage to the eye, with albendazole as the antiparasitic.
explain.table:
FormTypical ageFeatures
Visceral (VLM)Under 5Fever, wheeze, hepatomegaly, eosinophilia up to 70%
Ocular (OLM)5 to 10Unilateral vision loss, uveitis, chorioretinitis, mimics retinoblastoma, often no systemic signs
Neural (CNS)RareSeizures, neuropsychiatric symptoms, encephalopathy
why: Black fly-borne Onchocerca causes river blindness in adults near rivers in endemic areas, with skin nodules and itch.
An adult worm migrating under the conjunctiva is Loa loa in an adult from Central Africa.
Free-living amebae infect the cornea of contact lens wearers and cause a painful ulcer, not a retinal mass.
Cysticerci come from ingesting T. solium eggs, not from eating pork, and do not fit this pet exposure.
explain.takeaway: Ocular toxocariasis is a unilateral retinal lesion in a child 5 to 10 years old exposed to dog or cat feces; it can mimic retinoblastoma and often lacks eosinophilia.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Describe ocular toxocariasis and how it differs from the other forms of toxocariasis.

rows.if_right: years of itching and skin nodules in an adult from a West African river village

rows.if_right: Calabar swellings and a worm seen crossing the eye

questions.stem:
A 36-year-old woman who was born in New York City, has never traveled outside the United States, and keeps a strict vegetarian diet is brought to the emergency department after a first generalized seizure. CT of the head shows two small ring-enhancing cystic lesions in the cerebral cortex, and serology confirms a tapeworm infection of the brain. Her live-in housekeeper, who recently arrived from a rural pig-raising region of Central America, is later found to have tapeworm segments in her stool.

Which of the following best explains how this patient became infected?
choices: She ate undercooked pork containing larval cysts
She was bitten by a fly carrying infective larvae
Larvae penetrated her skin from contaminated soil
She ingested eggs shed in the housekeeper's feces
She ate raw freshwater fish containing larvae

explain.html:
With Taenia solium, the form that is swallowed decides the disease. Eating undercooked pork that contains cysticerci lets the larva attach by its scolex and grow into an adult tapeworm in the intestine (taeniasis), and that carrier then passes proglottids full of eggs in the stool. When a person instead ingests the eggs, the larvae cross the gut, enter the blood and lodge in muscle, eyes and brain, where they form cysticerci (neurocysticercosis). Neurocysticercosis therefore does not require eating pork, and household contacts of a carrier have about a 3-fold higher risk.

This patient never traveled and eats no meat, yet has seizures with ring-enhancing brain cysts. The decisive clue is her housekeeper with tapeworm segments in the stool: fecal contamination of food or hands carried that carrier's eggs to her. Finding and treating the tapeworm carrier in the household is what stops further cases.
explain.table:
What is ingestedWhere the parasite ends upDiseaseTreatment
Cysticerci (larvae) in undercooked porkAdult tapeworm attached to the intestine by its scolexTaeniasisPraziquantel
Eggs or proglottids from human fecesCysticerci in muscle, eyes and brain(Neuro)cysticercosisSteroids and albendazole
why: Pork containing cysticerci produces an intestinal tapeworm (taeniasis), not brain cysts, and she does not eat meat.
Fly bites transmit filarial worms, which cause skin, eye or blood findings rather than brain cysts.
Skin penetration from soil is the route of hookworm and Strongyloides, which do not form brain cysts.
Raw fish transmits the fish tapeworm, which stays in the intestine.
explain.takeaway: Neurocysticercosis follows ingestion of T. solium eggs shed by a human tapeworm carrier, so it occurs in people who never eat pork; eating cysticerci in pork causes only intestinal taeniasis.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Distinguish taeniasis, from eating cysticerci in pork, from neurocysticercosis, from ingesting Taenia solium eggs.

rows.why: Pork containing cysticerci produces an intestinal tapeworm (taeniasis), not brain cysts, and she does not eat meat.
rows.if_right: an intestinal tapeworm with proglottids in her own stool after eating undercooked pork

rows.why: Fly bites transmit filarial worms, which cause skin, eye or blood findings rather than brain cysts.
rows.if_right: Calabar swellings or a worm crossing the eye after years in a Central African rainforest (Loa loa)

rows.why: Skin penetration from soil is the route of hookworm and Strongyloides, which do not form brain cysts.
rows.if_right: a barefoot patient with an itchy foot track, cough, then iron deficiency anemia

rows.why: Raw fish transmits the fish tapeworm, which stays in the intestine.
rows.if_right: megaloblastic anemia in someone who eats raw fish from cold northern lakes

questions.stem:
A 61-year-old man from northern Finland comes to the clinic with fatigue, shortness of breath on exertion, and tingling in both feet. He regularly eats raw and lightly salted fish caught in cold local lakes. Hemoglobin is 9.0 g/dL (13.5 to 17.5) with a mean corpuscular volume of 118 fL (80 to 100), and a peripheral smear shows hypersegmented neutrophils. Stool ova and parasite examination shows operculated eggs, and he recalls passing long flat segments of worm.

Which of the following best explains his anemia?
choices: Adult worms ingest red blood cells in the small intestine
Macrophages in the spleen are filled with parasite forms
Larvae invade the bone marrow and replace normal cells
Chronic blood loss from colonic ulcers causes iron deficiency
The tapeworm competes for and absorbs dietary vitamin B12

explain.html:
Intestinal tapeworms are acquired as larvae in undercooked food, attach to the intestine by the scolex and usually cause only mild epigastric discomfort, nausea, flatulence or diarrhea. Proglottids release eggs that pass in feces, so stool O&P finds them, and praziquantel treats them. Diphyllobothrium latum, the fish tapeworm, comes from cold bodies of water in Northern Europe, North America and Japan; it reaches about 10 meters and can live 25 years.

What sets it apart is that the worm takes up vitamin B12 in the gut, and about 40% of patients develop megaloblastic anemia. This Finnish man who eats raw lake fish has passed flat segments and has a macrocytic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils and neuropathy, which is exactly the B12 picture. The anemia type separates this worm from hookworm, which causes a microcytic iron deficiency.
explain.table:
TapewormSourceDistinguishing feature
Diphyllobothrium latumRaw fish from cold water (N. Europe, N. America, Japan)Up to 10 m, lives 25 years, megaloblastic anemia in 40%
Taenia soliumPork (larvae) or human feces (eggs)Humans can be definitive or intermediate host; neurocysticercosis
Taenia saginataBeefHumans are definitive host only; longest Taenia, more symptoms from length
why: Blood feeding by adult worms in the small intestine is hookworm and causes a microcytic iron deficiency anemia, not macrocytosis.
Parasite-filled splenic macrophages are not a tapeworm feature and would not give hypersegmented neutrophils.
Intestinal tapeworm larvae do not invade the bone marrow; the adult stays attached in the gut.
Colonic blood loss gives iron deficiency with a low MCV, not an MCV of 118 fL.
explain.takeaway: Diphyllobothrium latum, acquired from raw fish in cold northern waters, absorbs vitamin B12 and causes megaloblastic anemia in about 40% of infected patients.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Compare the intestinal tapeworms: Diphyllobothrium latum, Taenia solium and Taenia saginata.

rows.why: Blood feeding by adult worms in the small intestine is hookworm and causes a microcytic iron deficiency anemia, not macrocytosis.
rows.if_right: a barefoot child with microcytic anemia, low ferritin and low albumin

questions.stem:
A 40-year-old woman from a sheep-raising region of South America comes to the clinic with 6 months of dull right upper quadrant fullness. Ultrasound shows a 12-cm cyst in the liver containing multiple smaller internal cysts. Serology is positive for the suspected cestode. A student on the team orders three stool ova and parasite examinations, and all are negative.

Which of the following best explains the negative stool studies?
choices: Eggs are shed only at night onto the perianal skin
Too few eggs are shed, so many more samples are needed
Humans carry only the larval cyst, never an egg-laying adult
Eggs are destroyed by gastric acid before reaching stool
Eggs are passed in urine rather than in the feces

explain.html:
Whether stool O&P can find a helminth depends on whether an egg-laying adult lives in the human gut. For Echinococcus, the adult tapeworm lives in the small intestine of dogs, the definitive host. Humans are incidental hosts who swallow eggs and develop only the larval hydatid cyst in liver or lung, so no eggs ever reach human stool.

This woman from a sheep-raising region has a 12-cm liver cyst with internal daughter cysts and positive serology, and her three negative stool exams are exactly what is expected. The diagnosis is made by imaging (ultrasound, CT) and serology, not O&P. Treatment depends on the stage of the liver cyst: resection if curative, and albendazole.
explain.table:
OrganismWhy stool O&P failsTest to use
EchinococcusHumans carry only the larval cystImaging (US, CT) and serology
EnterobiusEggs laid on perianal skinScotch tape test
ToxocaraLarvae never mature in the human gutSerology (ELISA)
StrongyloidesPoor sensitivity, needs 3 samplesSerology
TrichinellaLarvae encyst in muscleSerum antibody, muscle biopsy
why: Nocturnal perianal egg laying is pinworm, which causes itching, not a liver cyst.
No number of stool samples finds Echinococcus eggs in humans; the multiple-sample rule belongs to Strongyloides.
Gastric acid is not the reason; there is simply no adult worm in the human intestine to make eggs.
Eggs in urine describe urinary schistosomiasis, which presents with hematuria.
explain.takeaway: Humans carry only the larval hydatid cyst of Echinococcus, so stool O&P is negative; diagnose with imaging and serology and treat by stage with resection and albendazole.
explain.topic: Echinococcus: why stool testing fails and humans are dead-end hosts
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Explain why stool O&P is negative in echinococcosis and state how it is diagnosed and treated.

questions.stem:
A 4-year-old boy in a rural area with poor sanitation is brought to the clinic with colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, and abdominal distension. His mother noticed a large, pale, smooth worm about 20 cm long in his stool. Two months ago he had a week of dry cough and wheezing that resolved without treatment; a chest x-ray at that time showed transient patchy infiltrates, and the eosinophil count was elevated.

Which of the following best explains the earlier respiratory illness?
choices: Larvae penetrated the skin of his feet and reached the lungs
Antibodies to the adult worm cross-reacted with lung tissue
Eggs were inhaled in dust and hatched within the alveoli
Adult worms migrated up the esophagus into the trachea
Larvae hatched in the gut traveled via the liver to the lungs

explain.html:
Ascaris lumbricoides is a soil-transmitted helminth acquired by swallowing eggs from contaminated soil or vegetation. The eggs hatch in the gut, and the larvae cross the GI mucosa into the blood, reach the liver, then the lungs, climb the bronchi and are swallowed to become adult worms (15 to 30 cm) in the intestine: GUT, LIVER, LUNGS, GUT. When larvae reach the lungs, a few days to a week after infection, they cause Loeffler syndrome, an eosinophilic pneumonitis with wheeze, dyspnea, dry cough and transient pulmonary infiltrates.

This boy passed a 20-cm worm and now has obstructive symptoms, which heavy infection causes in children. His earlier week of wheeze with transient infiltrates and eosinophilia was the larval lung passage. Diagnosis is mammillated eggs on stool O&P, and treatment is albendazole.
explain.table:
NematodeEntryMigration
AscarisIngested eggsGUT, LIVER, LUNGS, GUT
Hookworm (Necator, Ancylostoma)Larvae penetrate skinSKIN, LUNGS, GUT
StrongyloidesLarvae penetrate skinSKIN, LUNGS, GUT, plus autoinfection
Enterobius, TrichurisIngested eggsNo lung phase
why: Skin penetration followed by lung passage is the route of hookworm and Strongyloides; Ascaris enters by swallowed eggs.
Loeffler syndrome comes from migrating larvae and eosinophils in the lung, not antibody cross-reactivity.
Ascaris eggs are swallowed and hatch in the gut; they are not inhaled.
Adult worms live in the intestine; the lung phase is larval and happened weeks earlier.
explain.takeaway: Ascaris larvae migrate GUT, LIVER, LUNGS, GUT, and their lung passage causes Loeffler syndrome: eosinophilic pneumonitis with wheeze and transient infiltrates.
explain.topic: Ascaris: larval migration through the lungs
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Trace the life cycle of Ascaris lumbricoides and explain Loeffler syndrome.

questions.stem:
A 12-year-old boy from a rural community with outdoor latrines and no indoor plumbing is brought to the clinic because of fatigue, poor school performance, and pallor. He usually goes barefoot. He has had no blood in his stool. Laboratory studies show:

[[labs 0]]

Stool microscopy shows thin-shelled oval eggs.

Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of his anemia?
choices: Vitamin B12 absorbed by a long intestinal tapeworm
Bleeding from flask-shaped ulcers in the colon
Hemolysis of red cells parasitized by protozoa
Marrow suppression caused by circulating microfilariae
Adult worms attached in the small intestine feed on blood

explain.html:
The human hookworms, Necator americanus and Ancylostoma duodenale, are soil-transmitted helminths spread where sanitation is poor: people defecating outside or using human feces as fertilizer, and others walking barefoot. Larvae penetrate the skin, enter the circulation, reach the alveoli, climb the trachea and are swallowed to mature in the small intestine (SKIN, LUNGS, GUT). The adults attach to the intestinal wall and constantly suck blood, producing iron deficiency anemia, and chronic heavy infection adds protein deficiency.

This barefoot boy from a community with outdoor latrines has a microcytic anemia with very low ferritin, low albumin, eosinophilia and thin-shelled oval eggs in stool. Diagnosis is eggs in stool and treatment is albendazole. In the southern United States, mass treatment once raised school enrollment, attendance, literacy and income.
explain.table:
WormMechanismAnemia type
Diphyllobothrium latumTakes up vitamin B12 in the gutMegaloblastic (macrocytic)
HookwormAdults suck blood in the small intestineIron deficiency (microcytic), plus protein loss
TrichurisColonic mucosal bleeding (bloody stool)Blood loss
why: Vitamin B12 uptake by the fish tapeworm causes a macrocytic anemia, not an MCV of 66 fL with low ferritin.
Flask-shaped colonic ulcers are amebiasis and cause bloody diarrhea, which he does not have.
Hemolysis from parasitized red cells is a protozoan picture and would not deplete ferritin or albumin.
Microfilariae circulate in the blood but do not suppress the bone marrow.
explain.takeaway: Hookworm larvae enter through bare skin (SKIN, LUNGS, GUT), and adults in the small intestine feed on blood, causing iron deficiency anemia and protein deficiency.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Describe hookworm transmission, life cycle and disease, including iron deficiency anemia.

questions.stem:
A 64-year-old man who worked as a coal miner in Appalachia is started on high-dose prednisone for a flare of an autoimmune disease. For years he has had intermittent epigastric pain, alternating diarrhea and constipation, and an itchy, linear rash on his buttocks that comes and goes. Three weeks after starting prednisone he develops fever, wheezing, hemoptysis, and abdominal pain, then becomes confused. Blood cultures grow Escherichia coli, and cerebrospinal fluid shows gram-negative rods.

Which of the following best explains the bacteremia and meningitis?
choices: Corticosteroids suppressed neutrophil production
Ruptured hydatid cyst seeded the blood with bacteria
Larvae penetrating the bowel wall carried enteric bacteria
Adult worms obstructed and perforated the intestine
Microfilariae in the blood triggered sepsis at night

explain.html:
Strongyloides stercoralis has an autoinfection cycle: rhabditiform larvae become filariform larvae inside the host and penetrate the gut mucosa or perianal skin, so infection can persist for decades. Chronic infection causes epigastric pain, intermittent diarrhea and constipation, mild eosinophilia, and recurrent itchy linear streaks (larva currens). Risk factors for acquiring it include contact with soil in farming or coal mining and living in Appalachia.

If high-dose corticosteroids, biologics, chemotherapy, HTLV-1, malignancy or HIV enter the picture, larval migration increases and larvae penetrate the bowel. Hyperinfection keeps them in the lungs and GI tract, while disseminated strongyloidiasis brings gram-negative rod bacteremia and meningitis, with 50 to 90% fatality. This retired coal miner with years of larva currens started prednisone and now has wheeze, hemoptysis, E. coli bacteremia and gram-negative meningitis: the larvae carried gut bacteria with them.
why: Steroids do not remove neutrophils, and enteric gram-negative bacteremia after years of larva currens points to the worm carrying gut flora.
Hydatid cyst rupture causes an allergic reaction or anaphylaxis, not gram-negative meningitis.
Intestinal obstruction from adult worms is an Ascaris complication of heavy infection in children.
Nocturnal microfilariae belong to lymphatic filariasis and do not cause bacteremia.
explain.takeaway: In chronic Strongyloides infection, corticosteroids trigger hyperinfection and dissemination, and larvae crossing the bowel carry gram-negative rods into the blood and meninges.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Explain Strongyloides autoinfection, hyperinfection and dissemination, and their risk factors.

rows.if_right: neutropenia after chemotherapy with no history suggesting a helminth

questions.stem:
A 3-year-old boy is brought to the clinic with 3 weeks of intermittent fever, cough with wheezing, and a decreased appetite. His parents have seen him eating dirt in the backyard, where the family's new puppies play. The liver edge is palpable 4 cm below the costal margin. Leukocyte count is 24,000/microL (4,500 to 11,000) with 52% eosinophils (1 to 4). Stool ova and parasite examination is negative.

Which of the following is the best test to confirm the diagnosis?
choices: Serum ELISA for antibodies to the larvae
Three more stool ova and parasite examinations
Scotch tape test of the perianal skin
Blood smear drawn at night for microfilariae
Sputum examination for operculated eggs

explain.html:
Toxocara canis and T. cati have dogs (puppies far more than older dogs) and cats as definitive hosts, and humans are incidental hosts. People ingest eggs from soil, sand, food or water, and the larvae disseminate, die and provoke eosinophilic inflammation. Visceral larva migrans, usually in children under 5, brings fever, cough and bronchospasm, abdominal pain, hepatomegaly and eosinophilia up to 70%.

This 3-year-old with pica, new puppies in the yard, wheeze, hepatomegaly and 52% eosinophils fits that picture. The larvae never mature in the human gut, so no eggs are released and stool O&P is not helpful. Diagnosis is serology by ELISA (sensitivity about 70 to 75%) or histology showing granulomas, and treatment is albendazole.
explain.table:
FormTypical ageFeatures
Visceral (VLM)Under 5Fever, wheeze, hepatomegaly, eosinophilia up to 70%
Ocular (OLM)5 to 10Unilateral vision loss, uveitis, chorioretinitis, mimics retinoblastoma, often no systemic signs
Neural (CNS)RareSeizures, neuropsychiatric symptoms, encephalopathy
why: More stool exams cannot find Toxocara because no eggs are released in the human gut.
The scotch tape test collects pinworm eggs from perianal skin.
A night smear finds Wuchereria and Brugia microfilariae, not Toxocara larvae.
Operculated eggs in sputum are a lung fluke feature and do not fit puppies, pica and hepatomegaly.
explain.takeaway: Toxocara visceral larva migrans (puppies, pica, hepatomegaly, marked eosinophilia) is diagnosed by serology, because the larvae never mature in humans and stool O&P is negative.

explain.objective: Describe Toxocara epidemiology, visceral larva migrans and its diagnosis.

questions.stem:
Three hunters come to the emergency department 10 days after sharing grilled bear meat cooked rare at a hunting camp. All have fever, severe muscle pain and tenderness, and swelling around both eyes; two had abdominal pain and diarrhea during the first week. Laboratory studies in one show eosinophils of 26% (1 to 4) and a markedly elevated creatine kinase.

Which of the following tests would best confirm the diagnosis?
choices: Stool ova and parasite examination
Lumbar puncture to count eosinophils in the CSF
Scotch tape test of the perianal skin
Skin snip biopsy placed in saline
Serum antibody testing or muscle biopsy

explain.html:
Trichinella spiralis is acquired by ingesting larvae in undercooked bear, pig or cougar meat. Early manifestations are fever, urticaria, eosinophilia, severe myalgias, abdominal pain and periorbital edema. The larvae travel to striated muscle and encyst, and involvement of the muscles around the eye produces the periorbital swelling.

Three hunters who shared rare bear meat now have fever, muscle pain, swelling around both eyes, 26% eosinophils and a high creatine kinase. Because the parasite lives in muscle, the diagnosis is serum antibody or muscle biopsy, and treatment is albendazole, plus steroids if severe. Cooking meat to an internal temperature of at least 165 F (74 C) prevents it.
why: Trichinella is on the list of helminths whose eggs are not found in stool; the disease lives in muscle.
CSF eosinophils point to Angiostrongylus or Baylisascaris, not this myositis picture.
The scotch tape test is for pinworm.
A skin snip in saline is the test for Onchocerca.
explain.takeaway: Trichinella (undercooked bear or pork: fever, myalgia, periorbital edema, eosinophilia) is confirmed by serology or muscle biopsy and treated with albendazole, plus steroids if severe.

explain.objective: Describe Trichinella spiralis transmission, presentation, diagnosis and treatment.

questions.stem:
A 30-year-old man who lived for several years in the rainforest region of Central Africa comes to the clinic with episodes of painless, nonred swelling of the forearm that last a few days and then move elsewhere. Last week he felt something crawling across his eye, and an ophthalmologist removed a thin worm from under the conjunctiva. A blood smear drawn at noon shows microfilariae at high density. Skin snips for other filariae are negative.

Which of the following is the major concern when choosing treatment?
choices: Diethylcarbamazine in heavy infection can cause brain inflammation
Praziquantel will cause rupture of hydatid cysts
Ivermectin will reverse established lymphedema
Doxycycline cannot kill the adult worms because they lack bacteria
Corticosteroids trigger dissemination of autoinfecting larvae

explain.html:
Loa loa, the African eye worm, is transmitted by the Chrysops fly in the rainforests of West and Central Africa and develops into adults only in humans. Adults move through subcutaneous connective tissue, causing transient Calabar swellings, and can migrate across the eye. They release microfilariae into the blood during the day, so diagnosis is the removed worm or a daytime blood smear.

Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) kills both microfilariae and adult worms, but with a heavy infection it carries a risk of brain inflammation after administration, and it should not be used where Onchocerca is endemic. This man has Calabar swellings, an eye worm and a high-density noon smear, so the heavy microfilarial load is the treatment decision that matters most.

Antihelminthics do not reverse lymphedema, and lymphedema belongs to Wuchereria and Brugia, not Loa loa.
Doxycycline acting on Wolbachia is the strategy for Onchocerca adults and is not the Loa loa concern here.
Steroid-triggered dissemination of autoinfecting larvae is a Strongyloides problem.
explain.takeaway: Loa loa (Chrysops fly, Calabar swellings, eye worm) is diagnosed by a daytime blood smear, and DEC treats it but can cause brain inflammation in heavy infection.

questions.stem:
A 38-year-old farmer from a West African village near a fast-flowing river comes to a clinic with years of intense itching that keeps him from working, thickened skin on his legs, and firm, painless nodules over his hips. His vision has gradually worsened. A slit-lamp examination shows inflammation and scarring of the cornea, and a skin snip biopsy placed in saline releases microfilariae. He is treated with ivermectin and doxycycline.

Doxycycline is included in the regimen because it does which of the following?
choices: Paralyzes the microfilariae circulating in the blood at night
Kills endosymbiotic bacteria that adult worms need to survive
Treats bacterial superinfection of the scratched skin
Prevents the brain inflammation caused by ivermectin
Blocks the black fly vector from transmitting larvae

explain.html:
Onchocerca volvulus is transmitted by black flies; larvae enter the bite wound and mature into adults that live in skin nodules and release microfilariae into the skin and eyes. In the skin they cause severe pruritus, sometimes so intense that people cannot work, and in the eyes inflammation and scarring cause river blindness. Diagnosis is a skin snip biopsy and a slit-lamp eye exam.

Treatment divides the work. Ivermectin kills microfilariae and sterilizes female worms but does not kill the adults. Doxycycline kills the adults indirectly by eliminating Wolbachia, the bacteria that live in adult worms and are essential to their development. This farmer has nodules, disabling itch, corneal scarring and microfilariae from a skin snip, and doxycycline is in his regimen to kill the adults through their endosymbiont.
explain.table:
DrugTarget in onchocerciasis
IvermectinKills microfilariae, sterilizes female worms
DoxycyclineKills Wolbachia, so the adult worms die
SurgeryRemoves nodules containing adults
why: Onchocerca microfilariae live in the skin, not night blood, and doxycycline does not target them.
Bacterial superinfection of scratched skin is not why doxycycline is part of this antiparasitic regimen.
The brain inflammation warning applies to diethylcarbamazine in heavy Loa loa infection.
Doxycycline acts on bacteria inside the worm, not on the black fly vector.
explain.takeaway: In onchocerciasis, ivermectin kills microfilariae and sterilizes females, while doxycycline kills the adult worms by eliminating their Wolbachia endosymbionts.

questions.stem:
A 45-year-old man from a coastal region of West Africa where both lymphatic filariasis and onchocerciasis are common comes to a clinic with progressive, nonpitting swelling of the left leg over several years, with thickened skin. He recalls frequent mosquito bites. A blood smear drawn at 11 PM shows microfilariae, and an antifilarial antibody test is positive.

Which of the following is the most appropriate antiparasitic treatment?
choices: Diethylcarbamazine alone
Albendazole plus ivermectin
Praziquantel alone
Triclabendazole alone
Metronidazole plus paromomycin

explain.html:
Lymphatic filariasis (elephantiasis) is caused 90% by Wuchereria bancrofti, with Brugia malayi, and is transmitted by mosquitoes. Adults live in the lymphatics and release microfilariae that circulate in lymph and blood at night (nighttime periodicity). Most people are asymptomatic, but in about 30% the lymphatics are damaged, and over years this produces lymphedema, mainly of the legs. Diagnosis is a night blood smear or an antifilarial antibody test.

Treatment depends on whether Onchocerca is also present. Without it, DEC is used; where Onchocerca is present, albendazole plus ivermectin is given. This man from a region where both are common has a midnight smear with microfilariae and leg lymphedema, so DEC is avoided. Antihelminthics will not reverse the lymphedema, because the lymphatic damage is permanent.

FilariaVectorAdultsMicrofilariaeTreatment
Wuchereria, BrugiaMosquitoLymphaticsBlood at nightDEC; albendazole plus ivermectin if Onchocerca present
Loa loaChrysops flySubcutaneous, movingBlood during the dayDEC (brain inflammation risk if heavy)
Onchocerca volvulusBlack flySkin nodulesSkinIvermectin plus doxycycline
why: DEC alone is the choice only when Onchocerca is absent, and this region has both.
Praziquantel treats tapeworms and flukes, not filarial worms.
Triclabendazole is a fluke drug and has no role in filariasis.
Metronidazole plus paromomycin treats amebiasis.
explain.takeaway: Lymphatic filariasis (mosquito, night blood smear) is treated with DEC if Onchocerca is absent or albendazole plus ivermectin if present, and neither reverses lymphedema.

questions.stem:
A clinic in a rural community with outdoor latrines evaluates five patients, all with peripheral eosinophilia. Patient 1 is a 3-year-old with fever, wheezing and hepatomegaly who eats dirt in a yard where puppies play. Patient 2 is a 6-year-old with nocturnal perianal itching that her siblings share. Patient 3 is a 40-year-old sheep herder with a large liver cyst containing daughter cysts on CT. Patient 4 is a 5-year-old with bloody diarrhea, weight loss and rectal prolapse. Patient 5 is a hunter with fever, severe myalgia and periorbital edema after eating rare bear meat. A visiting student proposes a stool ova and parasite examination for everyone.

For which patient is the stool ova and parasite examination most likely to show the organism's eggs?
choices: Patient 1
Patient 3
Patient 2
Patient 4
Patient 5

explain.html:
A stool O&P detects eggs, so it works only when egg-laying adults live in the human gut lumen and release eggs into feces. Many helminths fail that test. When the human is an incidental or intermediate host, only larvae are present: Toxocara larvae wander and die in tissue, and in hydatid disease the human holds the cyst while the adult tapeworm lives in the dog. Trichinella larvae encyst in striated muscle and are found by antibody or muscle biopsy. Pinworm adults do live in the cecum, but females lay eggs on the perianal skin at night, so the scotch tape test is used.

The 5-year-old with bloody diarrhea and rectal prolapse has whipworm (Trichuris trichiura). Its adults live in the large intestine, cecum and appendix, and stool O&P shows eggs with plugged ends. The pinworm patient is the trap: an intestinal worm whose eggs still do not reach the stool.

questions.stem:
A 45-year-old man from a region where lymphatic filariasis is common and onchocerciasis does not occur has had progressive swelling of his left leg for 8 years, now with thickened skin. He has no itching and no eye symptoms. A blood smear drawn at 11 PM shows microfilariae, and an antifilarial antibody test is positive. He is treated with diethylcarbamazine (DEC). The clinician explains that DEC kills both microfilariae and adult worms, and the patient asks whether his leg will finally go back to its old size once the worms are gone.

Six months after successful treatment, which pair of findings is most likely?
choices: Microfilariae on a night smear; the leg back to its normal size
No microfilariae on a night smear; the leg back to its normal size
No microfilariae in blood, but microfilariae now found on skin snip
Microfilariae on a night smear but none on a smear taken at midday
No microfilariae on a night smear; the leg still as swollen

explain.html:
In lymphatic filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia), mosquitoes transmit larvae, adults live in the lymphatics, and microfilariae circulate in the blood at night. Most infected people have no symptoms, but in about a third the lymphatics are damaged, and over many years lymphedema and elephantiasis develop, mainly in the legs. Diagnosis is a night blood smear or antifilarial antibody; treatment is DEC when onchocerciasis is absent, or albendazole plus ivermectin when it is present. Antihelminthics do not reverse damage to the lymphatics.

For this man, success means the parasite is gone, so the night smear becomes negative. The leg, though, reflects 8 years of lymphatic damage that persists after the worms die, so it stays swollen. The clinician's point that DEC kills adult worms is true but does not change that, and day versus night or skin findings belong to Loa loa and Onchocerca.

why: After successful DEC the blood should be cleared of microfilariae, and killing worms would not shrink the leg anyway.
The smear does clear, but the swelling comes from damaged lymphatics, which killing the worms does not repair.
Microfilariae in skin are Onchocerca, which is absent here; Wuchereria microfilariae do not move into the skin after treatment.
Wuchereria microfilariae circulate at night regardless of treatment; the day versus night contrast describes Loa loa versus Wuchereria, not a treatment response.
explain.takeaway: In lymphatic filariasis, DEC clears Wuchereria or Brugia (night smear turns negative) but does not reverse lymphedema from years of lymphatic damage by adult worms.
